docs.title: FISS Planner
docs.text:
Fast Iterative Search and Sampling trajectory planners for autonomous driving: FISS (RA-L 2022) and FISS+ (IROS 2023), with the FOP and FOP+ baselines, in one C++17 core with Python bindings and ROS 1 / ROS 2 nodes, Lanelet2 / CommonRoad / CARLA support, an optional QP smoother and an MPC controller.

▶ Interactive replay: step through CommonRoad scenarios with every planner, including the candidate trajectories each one explored.

  • Concepts: reference line, corridor, sampling, the four search strategies, validation, smoothing, stitching and control.
  • Python: pip install fiss-planner, planners, LocalPlanner, maps, controllers.
  • ROS: nodes, topics, parameters, Lanelet2, runtime switching.
  • Benchmarks: CommonRoad, ROS 2 bag replay and CARLA results, and how to reproduce them.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: All numbers were measured on one machine: an Intel Core i9-12900K (24 threads) with an RTX 3090 Ti for CARLA, running Ubuntu 24.04. Each planning cycle runs on a single core. Raw per-run results are in benchmarks/results/.

docs.title: Profiles, splits and tuning
docs.text:
Each benchmark runs with its own planner profile (python/fiss_planner/profiles/, chosen with --profile), and every result records the profile and a hash of the resolved settings. A profile is tuned only on its benchmark's development split and checked on a second held-out split. The test split is run once per release.

Benchmark Profile Tuning split Check split Test split CommonRoad commonroad benchmarks/commonroad/dev_set.txt (100 hand-crafted) check_set.txt (103 hand-crafted) bench_set.txt (280) CARLA scenarios carla_scenarios – – lead vehicle, parked car, cut-in; traffic seeds 0–9 nuPlan nuplan mini_dev14 (Val14 filter on 44 mini logs of the train split) – Val14, Test14-hard Bench2Drive bench2drive bench2drive_0.0.4_val (220 routes) – bench2drive220 (220 routes)

The CommonRoad splits are disjoint, and the benchmark reads them directly (--scenarios benchmarks/commonroad/dev_set.txt). Tuning uses Optuna (TPE) over a search space declared per benchmark in benchmarks/tuning/, and the first trial is the current profile:

python benchmarks/tune.py benchmarks/tuning/commonroad.yaml --trials 60 --jobs 16 --out results/tune/commonroad

The tuner writes three things: the best settings as a complete profile with their provenance, a table of all trials, and the scores of the current and the best profile on the check split. It refuses test splits.

docs.title: CommonRoad, closed loop
docs.text:
Scenarios. The set is 280 public scenarios from commonroad-scenarios (commit 2416dc2): all 130 NGSIM recordings (US-101, Lankershim, Peachtree) and 150 hand-crafted scenarios drawn with seed 0 (list in benchmarks/commonroad/bench_set.txt).

Protocol. - At every 0.1 s step the planner receives the ego state and all obstacles, then the ego moves to its planned state one step later (perfect tracking, as in the FISS / FISS+ papers). - Traffic is the recorded, non-reactive log. - Obstacle predictions are ground truth unless stated otherwise. - The vehicle is CommonRoad's VW Vanagon, and the grid is 5×5×5 per lane. - The route comes from CommonRoad's route planner. The planner's goal point, where the route's lane changes must be done, is the point of the goal region the ego would pass in the middle of the time window at its initial speed, kept one second of driving inside the region's ends. The target speed brings the ego there in time, given that the planner reaches a new speed within its mean horizon, and stays within the goal speed interval.

Metrics. - Success: the official GoalRegion.is_reached check, covering position, time window, speed and heading, with no collision and no road-boundary violation (CommonRoad drivability checker). - Headway < 1 s: time per scenario spent less than 1 s behind the vehicle ahead in the ego's path, while keeping the lane (overtaking pull-outs excluded). - Min TTC < 2 s: share of scenarios whose minimum time to collision with that vehicle drops below 2 s. - Within 0.5 m: share of scenarios in which the ego's footprint comes within 0.5 m of another road user's at the same instant.

Weights and thresholds of the distance keeping were fixed a priori (1.5 s desired headway, 4 s desired TTC, 2 m / 1.5 s hard floor) and checked on a separate development set of 100 hand-crafted scenarios that are not part of the benchmark; they were not tuned on these 280. The time gap to crossing traffic (0.75 s) was chosen on the development set as well. The route urgency (a 10 s ramp per lane change), the reference smoothing (20 m, 0.1 m) and the goal point were set a priori and checked on the development set and on 103 further hand-crafted scenarios outside the benchmark (zipper merges, highway and urban scenes, T-junctions). The two sets are listed in benchmarks/commonroad/dev_set.txt and check_set.txt.

The four search strategies reach practically the same solutions. FISS generates about 11× fewer trajectories than FOP and plans about 14× faster. The QP smoother adds 9–10 points of success, mostly by converting timeouts.

Most of the remaining failures are timeouts in the NGSIM recordings, whose goals combine a place, a time window of 0.1–1 s and a speed interval in dense traffic. All collisions of FISS+ with the QP smoother except the two short urban scenarios (ZAM_Urban-4/5_1_S-1, within 1.2 s of the start) are recorded vehicles running into the ego from behind: three times while it waits at a red light, once after it brakes with a faster vehicle closing in behind. Replayed traffic cannot react to the ego.

docs.title: Ablations (fiss_plus with the QP smoother)
docs.text:
Variant Success Collision Timeout Headway < 1 s Min TTC < 2 s Within 0.5 m default: ego and adjacent lanes, ground-truth prediction 74.6 % 2.1 % 18.2 % 0.14 s 12.1 % 7.9 % without the safety envelope and proximity cost 80.4 % 2.1 % 12.9 % 0.47 s 22.5 % 20.7 % ego lane only (as in the papers) 67.1 % 3.9 % 24.3 % 0.23 s 17.5 % 8.6 % lane-following prediction 70.7 % 8.6 % 13.6 % 0.13 s 1.1 % 10.0 % constant-velocity prediction 69.3 % 10.0 % 14.6 % 0.12 s 1.4 % 9.3 %
  • Keeping distance cuts the time spent below 1 s of headway to under a third, the share of runs that get within 2 s TTC of the vehicle ahead almost by half, and the share that come within 0.5 m of another road user by more than half, at the same collision rate. In the replayed logs it costs 5.8 points of success: 18 runs in dense NGSIM traffic time out because the gaps their lane changes need before the goal window closes are refused, and recorded traffic does not open them.
  • Route lane changes. The planner counts the lane changes the route still needs and makes them in time for the goal: several changes start earlier than one, and a slower target lane does not hold them back once they are due (see route urgency).
  • Turning across traffic. The time gap to crossing and oncoming vehicles is part of the safety envelope. On the development set it brings the runs within 0.5 m of another vehicle from 30 to 0 (of 100) at the same success rate. In the T-junction of the gallery (ZAM_Tjunction-1_101) the closest approach during the left turn grows from 0.3 m to 1.0 m, and the time gap from 0.2 s to 1.0 s. Larger gaps backfire in replayed logs, where traffic does not yield: the ego starts to give way and then stops in the vehicle's path. At 1 s one development scenario ends in a collision, at 1.5 s five do.
  • Map-aware lane sampling (adjacent lanes) avoids conflicts the ego lane alone cannot.
  • Prediction. With predictions from the current state only, as a deployed system has them, lane-following prediction gains 1.4 points of success over constant-velocity prediction, with 8.6 % instead of 10.0 % collisions. Recorded traffic still does not react to the ego, so the remaining gap to ground-truth predictions is largely the replay itself. TTC values are measured from each cycle's predictions, so they are comparable within a prediction mode only.

docs.title: ROS 2 bag replay (open loop)
docs.text:
fiss_planner.bags.from_commonroad turns NGSIM recordings into MCAP bags. A logged vehicle is the ego (/odom), its lane chain is the reference (/planning/reference_path), and all other traffic is published with constant-velocity predictions (/perception/obstacles). bag_replay_eval.py plays each bag through the real ROS 2 node (plan_on_odom, sim time) and compares every plan with where the logged driver went.

Planner Cycles with a plan Emergency stops ADE 3 s FDE 3 s Node cycle mean / p95 fop 84.0 % 3.8 % 1.45 m 4.02 m 10.9 / 17.1 ms fop_plus 83.6 % 3.7 % 1.37 m 3.96 m 3.2 / 6.7 ms fiss 83.3 % 3.6 % 1.33 m 4.33 m 2.6 / 7.3 ms fiss_plus 83.2 % 3.2 % 1.29 m 4.21 m 2.4 / 5.7 ms

The replay is open loop: the ego follows the log, not the plan. A missing plan therefore mostly means the logged driver's situation, for example a gap closing under constant-velocity prediction, violates the planner's margins.

docs.title: CARLA
docs.text:
CARLA 0.9.16 runs headless and synchronously (20 Hz physics) on Town04. Every 0.1 s the planner gets the ego state, the CARLA map as a RoadMap, with lane-change rules from the road markings and the route from CARLA's GlobalRoutePlanner, and all actors with lane-following predictions on that map. CARLA traffic reacts to the ego, so followers in its own lane are left to keep their distance (ignore_rear_in_lane). The controller tracks the plan at 20 Hz. Collisions and lane invasions come from CARLA sensors; time headway and time to collision are measured to the vehicle ahead in the ego's path every planning cycle.

Scenarios: - lead vehicle: a slower car ahead. - parked car: a stopped car in the ego lane. - cut-in: a scripted car drives at 9 m/s in the adjacent lane, then merges into the ego lane 8–20 m ahead within 2.5 s. - traffic: 49 Traffic Manager vehicles, 60 s along a cross-map route.

Chase camera Bird's-eye (planner view)

Full-length videos (cut-in, parked car, traffic) are attached to the GitHub release; regenerate them with python -m fiss_planner.carla.record --scenario <name> --mp4 <file>.

The Stanley+PID runs are in the JSON file; they give the same picture. Minimum TTC and headway are measured to the vehicle ahead while keeping the lane. The scripted cut-in merges 8–20 m ahead within 2.5 s, closing at several metres per second: every planner brakes (the emergency cycles), then follows or moves over a lane, without a collision. It is the tightest scenario. When the car merges, no plan can keep the safety envelope; the retry that keeps it as a cost then brakes firmly towards the car's speed, and the closest approach (box to box) is 0.5–0.8 m over all planners and both controllers. Varying the reference line by a few centimetres keeps the FISS+ result between 0.6 m and 0.9 m.

docs.title: Dense traffic, ten seeds (FISS+, MPC)
docs.text:
Traffic Manager behaviour differs from run to run, so configurations are compared over ten seeds of the 60 s traffic scenario rather than single runs. The second row switches off map-aware prediction, distance keeping, the rear-vehicle rule and the fallback retries.

Configuration Runs Collisions Plan success Emergency Fallback Headway < 1 s Median min TTC Distance Plan time default 10 0 99.5 % 0.00 % 0.50 % 0.00 s 4.03 s 666 m 0.42 ms constant-velocity prediction, no distance keeping, no rear rule, no retries 10 0 99.8 % 0.05 % 0.20 % 4.66 s 4.07 s 672 m 0.54 ms

Both configurations plan almost every cycle. Without distance keeping the ego spends 4.7 s per run less than 1 s behind the vehicle ahead, with the defaults none, and its predictions of vehicles in the next lane sweep across its own lane instead of following theirs. The routes cross the town, and the ego takes their turns at junctions.

Two runs end in a jam: in seed 7 the ego queues behind a stopped car, in seed 9 it waits at a junction for traffic crossing its path. It comes to rest about 3.5 m behind the stopped car (the desired gap is 3 m) and plans 98.7 % and 97.5 % of the cycles of these runs; the other eight plan 99.9 %, with no emergency braking.

Scenario Controller Collisions Lateral error RMS Along-track lag RMS cruise mpc 0 1.4 cm 1.04 m cruise stanley_pid 0 12.4 cm 0.85 m parked car mpc 0 1.5 cm 1.05 m parked car stanley_pid 0 12.6 cm 0.85 m cut-in (scripted) mpc 0 0.8 cm 0.87 m cut-in (scripted) stanley_pid 0 6.5 cm 0.70 m traffic (30 s) mpc 0 1.1 cm 1.01 m traffic (30 s) stanley_pid 0 8.5 cm 0.98 m

Lane invasions are not shown in the tables because evasive lane changes and overtakes trigger them by design. They are included in the JSON files. The along-track lag is mostly the 0.05 s latency compensation in the stitching plus the simple throttle/brake mapping of the runner (Actuation); lateral tracking is the controller's job, and the MPC holds it to 1–2 cm.

docs.title: Frenet frame and reference line
docs.text:
ReferenceLine is an arc-length parameterized cubic spline through a polyline (any number of points; it extends straight past both ends). It converts full kinematic states exactly between Cartesian (x, y, yaw, v, a, kappa) and time-domain Frenet (s, ṡ, s̈, d, ḋ, d̈); heading and curvature of planned trajectories come from the analytic velocity and acceleration vectors.

Map centerlines are often noisy: digitized or recorded lanes carry vertices a few centimetres off the line, sometimes nearly on top of each other. An interpolating spline turns that into curvature spikes, which cap the speed (through the curvature limit) and jolt the Cartesian acceleration of planned trajectories. With a map, the lane chain is therefore first smoothed (smoothPolyline): resampled every metre, fitted with a second-difference penalty that removes wiggles shorter than route.smoothing_length (20 m), and reweighted until no point moves more than route.smoothing_tolerance (0.1 m), so real curves keep their shape. On the NGSIM US-101 lanes this lowers the 95th-percentile curvature from 0.017 to 0.002 1/m. Paths given with setReferencePath are used as they are.

docs.title: Corridor and lanes
docs.text:
A Corridor is a set of lane bands [right(s), left(s)] expressed in the reference frame. With a map, buildRouteCorridor follows the ego's lane chain along the route and adds adjacent lanes using their real boundaries, so curved and merging lanes keep their geometry. Each band carries:

  • change_allowed: whether the ego may enter it (line markings or the routing graph; a route through the neighbour implies the change is legal);
  • extra_cost and urgency: the route's claim on the lane (below);
  • speed_limit.

The union of allowed lanes is the road boundary used by the off-road check. Active stop lines (red lights) become virtual static obstacles.

Route urgency. The route is a list of lane ids in driving order that ends in the destination lane; setMap optionally takes a goal point in that lane. Along each band the planner looks for the points where the band cannot go on as it is, also beyond the reference line:

  • where a route lane leaves the route: the route's lane changes from there are due, until it continues lengthwise;
  • where a band off the route ends or can no longer reach the route over permitted changes: the changes back to it are due;
  • at the end of a dead-end road, and at the goal: the changes into the lane the route continues in, or into the destination lane.

For n changes due in a distance D, with U = max(urgency_distance, urgency_time · v) (80 m, 10 s), the urgency is u = clamp(1 − D / (n·U), 0, 1) and the cost w_route_urgency · n · u / (1 − u) (w = 10, capped at 10 w n): nothing while the changes fit comfortably, w · n with half a ramp per change left, then quickly more. The more changes are needed, the earlier they start, and changes further along the route wait for their own deadlines. A band takes its most urgent deadline. Lanes off the route cost another w, so leaving the route to pass slower traffic has to be worth it.

docs.title: Sampling and cost
docs.text: End states form a grid over lateral offset (num_width samples per allowed lane) × target speed × horizon. Lateral motion is a quintic and longitudinal motion a quartic polynomial. The cost follows Werling et al.: horizon, terminal speed error, terminal offset from the lane center and lane-change/urgency costs (all known from the end state), plus mean squared acceleration and jerk. The end-state part is a lower bound of the full cost, which FISS uses as its heuristic.

docs.title: Keeping distance
docs.text:
Obstacles are projected into the Frenet frame once per cycle (extent [s_min, s_max] × [d_min, d_max] and along-track speed on a 0.5 s grid), so the terms below are cheap interval tests for every candidate. Gap and time-to-collision rules apply to obstacles moving along the reference line (within 45°) or standing still; crossing and oncoming traffic is left to the collision check.

Car following. Per lane, the vehicle ahead sets a following speed v_lead + (gap − (desired_gap + desired_time_headway · v_lead)) / follow_time. Candidates ending in that lane are scored against it instead of the desired speed, so the speed term no longer pulls the ego into the vehicle ahead. The lane's deficit to the desired speed is charged as a lane cost, so a free neighbouring lane stays attractive and the ego overtakes when that pays off. This cost fades with the urgency of the ego lane (1 − u): a faster lane that the route requires leaving does not hold back the change into a slower one.

Following and stopping (Werling et al., sampling.follow_lead). Besides the grid, every cycle tries candidates in the ego lane that end behind the vehicle ahead at its speed after T = 1 s, 2 s, … max_t, at the desired gap (desired_gap + desired_time_headway · v) or just outside the safety envelope (0.5 m beyond its gap), and continue at that speed. Behind a stopped vehicle or an active stop line they stop at that gap instead, over the time a constant deceleration would take (never shorter than the deceleration limit allows); from rest they stay or creep up to the gap. Their position-controlled ends and short durations give firm braking and exact stops the grid's speed-controlled samples (3–5 s) cannot. The cheapest valid candidate of grid and follower wins, in all four planners alike.

Proximity cost (CostTerms.proximity, per-sample means like the comfort terms):

Term Penalizes Default w_headway gap ahead below desired_gap + desired_time_headway · v 10, 3 m + 1.5 s w_ttc time to collision with the vehicle ahead below desired_ttc 5, 4 s w_clearance lateral gap to an obstacle alongside below desired_clearance 5, 1 m

Each term is (1 − actual / desired)² when positive and 0 otherwise; obstacles behind the ego are ignored. Because it is computed when a candidate is generated and is never negative, the lazy planners still validate in exact cost order.

Safety envelope (SafetyConfig, a hard "virtual bumper"): a candidate is rejected (safety_distance) if its gap to an obstacle ahead in its path falls below min_gap + min_time_headway · v (2 m + 0.3 s) or its time to collision below min_ttc (1.5 s). An obstacle already in the path, or one that cuts into the ego's lane, is checked only from reaction_time (0.5 s) after it appears and may not be approached closer than it appeared, so after a close cut-in the braking candidates stay feasible. Lane changes towards an obstacle get no such grace; samples that move laterally away from an obstacle (pulling out to overtake) are held to its time to collision but not to the gap floor, so an overtake that cannot be completed still leaves room to brake. Standing still never breaches the gap floor (it closes no gap), so a vehicle that came to rest too close may stay. The optional QP smoother respects the same envelope.

Turning across traffic. The gap and TTC rules cover traffic heading within 45° of the ego. Towards crossing and oncoming vehicles the envelope is a post-encroachment time instead: a candidate may not occupy space such a vehicle occupies within crossing_time_gap (0.75 s) before or after it, so an unprotected left turn either waits for a gap or goes clearly ahead, instead of squeezing past within the collision margin. Like the other envelope rules it gives way when no candidate satisfies it (see the fallbacks below), so the rule alone never forces a stop halfway through a turn.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text: Obstacles carry their own predicted states, so any predictor can be plugged in. predictLaneFollowing moves an obstacle along its lane of a RoadMap at constant speed (straightest successor at forks), decaying its lateral offset to the centerline; it falls back to constant velocity off the map, when the obstacle is not heading along its lane, or when it is nearly stopped. completePredictions gives every moving obstacle that arrives with only its current state (as tracked objects from perception usually do) such a prediction; the ROS nodes apply it according to prediction.mode.

docs.title: The four planners
docs.text:
Generates Validates FOP all candidates all candidates (optionally in parallel) FOP+ all candidates in cost order until one passes FISS lazily, along a discrete gradient descent over the grid, guided by the previous cycle's solution the cheapest generated candidate; repeat FISS+ lazily, by best-first neighbour exploration; then continuous refinement of the end state with a decaying step the cheapest generated candidate; refined candidates if they beat it

All four return the same kind of Trajectory and share every check.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A candidate is accepted if it is finite and within speed, acceleration, curvature and lateral-acceleration limits, stays inside the road bounds (heading-aware footprint), respects the safety envelope, and its inflated box does not overlap any obstacle's predicted box at the same time (separating-axis test with a circle pre-check). A start state already at or beyond a limit (e.g. stitched onto a full stop) may not get worse rather than failing outright. Below 1 m/s, where curvature is not checked, a candidate may not move more sideways than along the lane (more than 45° off it): a car cannot crab. Samples slower than 0.05 m/s keep the heading they came with, since the direction of so small a velocity means nothing.

With collision.ignore_rear_in_lane (on in the CARLA runner and the ROS configs), lane-keeping candidates ignore obstacles that start behind the ego in its own lane: with traffic that reacts, the follower keeps its distance. Lane changes still check them.

Every rejection is counted per reason (PlanStats.rejections), and the obstacle that rejected the cheapest candidate is reported as PlanStats.blocking_id (with blocking_t), together with the gap, time headway and time to collision of the vehicle ahead (PlanStats.lead).

docs.title: Smoothing (optional)
docs.text: The chosen trajectory defines a space–time corridor: at every time, the lateral interval free of road edges and of obstacles on the side it passes them, and the longitudinal interval free of obstacles sharing its lateral band. Two piecewise-jerk QPs (lateral, then longitudinal; OSQP) smooth the trajectory inside that corridor while keeping the sampled speed profile's timing. The result is used only if it passes the same validation.

docs.title: Stitching and fail-safes
docs.text:
LocalPlanner plans from the previous trajectory at t + latency while the vehicle tracks it within tolerance (otherwise from the measured state). If no candidate is valid, it falls back in this order:

  1. keep the rest of the previous plan while it is still collision free (fallback);
  2. if the safety envelope rejected candidates, re-plan with the envelope as a cost instead of a check, with the full collision check: a close but collision-free plan is safer than hard braking in traffic, and the one that breaches the envelope least wins (degraded). The breach is the worst relative shortfall of the gap below its floor or of the time to collision below min_ttc, charged at envelope_retry_weight (1000) per unit, so after a close cut-in the retry brakes firmly instead of comfortably;
  3. re-plan the same way with collisions checked only over the first degraded_horizon seconds (2.5 s), since long-horizon predictions are the least reliable (degraded);
  4. brake at the limit in its lane (emergency).

After an emergency stop the next plan starts from the measured state, with its initial deceleration capped at recovery_decel (2 m/s²): stitching onto the stop profile would carry full braking into every new plan and bring the vehicle to a standstill even once the way is clear. Likewise, below 1 m/s plans start with at most the deceleration 3 v / max_t, with which a polynomial stop within the horizon does not back up: a vehicle coming to rest does not keep decelerating once it stands.

docs.title: Control
docs.text: MpcController is a linear time-varying MPC on kinematic-bicycle error dynamics (lateral, heading, along-track and speed errors) with steering angle/rate and acceleration limits. StanleyPidController is the simple baseline. Both track the time-parameterized trajectory.

docs.title: Inspecting runs in Foxglove
docs.text:
Every CARLA and CommonRoad run can be written to an MCAP file, or streamed live, and opened in Foxglove or the open-source Lichtblick. Scrub through a run frame by frame and see what the planner saw: every candidate with its cost rank, the obstacle that blocked the cheapest candidate, the predicted paths, gap / headway / time to collision to the vehicle ahead, planning times and (in CARLA) the camera.

The recordings of the demo runs are attached to the GitHub release (carla_cut_in.mcap, carla_traffic.mcap, commonroad_zip.mcap).

docs.title: Open a recording
docs.text:
1. Download a .mcap file and the layout docs/foxglove/fiss_planner_layout.json.
  2. Open the file in Foxglove (desktop app or app.foxglove.dev; a free account is required) or Lichtblick.
  3. Import the layout (Layouts → Import from file).

The layout shows a 3D view following the ego, the camera, plots of speed vs. target, headway and TTC, planning time and trajectory count, and the raw planner statistics.

Topic Content /map/lanes lane boundaries /ego ego box and heading /obstacles obstacle boxes and predicted paths; vehicle ahead yellow, blocking obstacle orange /plan/trajectory executed plan /plan/candidates explored candidates, cheapest brightest; rejected ones faint /plan/stats JSON: planner, mode (plan / fallback / degraded / emergency), timings, counts, gap, headway, TTC, rejections /tf map → ego /camera/image JPEG chase camera (CARLA)

docs.title: Record your own
docs.text:
pip install "fiss-planner[foxglove,commonroad]"
# CommonRoad scenario
python -m fiss_planner.commonroad.demo ZAM_Zip-1_50_T-1.xml --mcap zip.mcap
# CARLA with the chase camera (start the simulator first)
python -m fiss_planner.carla.record --scenario cut_in --mcap cut_in.mcap
# CARLA batch runs, one file per run
python -m fiss_planner.carla.closed_loop --scenario traffic --mcap recordings/

Add --foxglove-live to the CARLA commands and connect Foxglove to ws://localhost:8765 to watch a run while it drives. For the ROS nodes, record the topics with ros2 bag record -s mcap (see ROS).

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
pip install fiss-planner               # bindings, smoother and MPC included
pip install "fiss-planner[commonroad]" # CommonRoad adapter and benchmark

docs.title: A single planning call
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import fiss_planner as fp

x = np.arange(0.0, 300.0, 5.0)
ref = fp.ReferenceLine(x, np.zeros_like(x))
lanes = fp.Corridor.parallel_lanes(0.0, ref.length, 3.5, 1, 0)
obstacles = [fp.predict_constant_velocity(1, 45.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 4.5, 1.9, horizon=6.0, dt=0.1)]

cfg = fp.make_config("fiss_plus", num_width=5)
cfg.cost.w_lane_change = 3.0
planner = fp.make_planner(cfg, fp.VehicleParams())
res = planner.plan(fp.FrenetState(s=10.0, s_d=10.0), ref, lanes, obstacles, target_speed=12.0)
traj = res.trajectory            # numpy arrays: traj.t, traj.x, traj.y, traj.yaw, traj.v, traj.kappa, traj.s, traj.d …
print(res.stats.rejections)      # why candidates were rejected
print(res.stats.lead.gap, res.stats.lead.ttc, res.stats.blocking_id)  # vehicle ahead; what blocked

Keeping distance is configured on the same object (see Concepts):

cfg.cost.desired_time_headway = 2.0   # comfort: car following and proximity cost
cfg.safety.min_ttc = 2.0              # hard envelope ("virtual bumper")

docs.title: The full pipeline
docs.text:
lp = fp.LocalPlanner(fp.LocalPlannerConfig(), fp.VehicleParams())
lp.set_map(road_map, route_lane_ids, goal=(gx, gy))  # or lp.set_reference_path(xs, ys)
out = lp.step(t, fp.EgoState(x, y, yaw, v), obstacles)
lp.request_planner_type(fp.PlannerType.FOP)  # takes effect next cycle

road_map is an fp.RoadMap of fp.MapLanes; adapters build it from CommonRoad (fiss_planner.commonroad.road_map_from_lanelet_network) and CARLA (fiss_planner.carla.adapter.road_map_from_carla). The route lists lane ids in driving order and ends in the destination lane; the optional goal, a point in that lane, is where the route's lane changes must be done (see route urgency).

docs.title: Configuration files and profiles
docs.text:
Every LocalPlannerConfig setting has a YAML key named after its field, the same as the ROS 2 parameter: the scalars (desired_speed, degraded_horizon, ...) at the top level, then the sections planner, sampling, cost, constraints, collision, safety, fiss_plus, route, stitching, path, behavior, free_space, smoother and vehicle. Missing keys keep their defaults and unknown keys raise an error.

cfg, vehicle = fp.load_local_planner_config("my_config.yaml", vehicle)  # fields not in the file keep their value
print(fp.to_yaml(cfg))                                                   # every setting; reads back exactly

A profile is such a file with every setting pinned, tuned for one benchmark or simulator. The shipped profiles are commonroad and carla_scenarios (see Benchmarks):

cfg, vehicle = fp.profiles.load("carla_scenarios", vehicle)
cfg, vehicle = fp.profiles.override(cfg, vehicle, {"cost.w_lane_change": 3.0, "desired_speed": 12.0})
fp.profiles.config_hash(cfg, vehicle)  # fingerprint the benchmarks record with every result

docs.title: Free space (parking)
docs.text:
With cfg.free_space.enabled, a LocalPlanner on a map that finds the vehicle at low speed outside every lane of its corridor (parked on a strip, on a shoulder) plans a Hybrid A* path, forwards and backwards, across the map's lanes and areas back into its lane, then hands over to the lane planner. Add the drivable space outside the lanes with road_map.add_area(polygon). While it drives free space, out.free_space is set, out.free_space_path holds the path and the trajectory's speed is negative where it reverses. The search is also available on its own:

grid = fp.OccupancyGrid(cx, cy, 50.0, 0.1)   # starts occupied
grid.mark_free(lane_polygon)                 # (N, 2) arrays
grid.mark_occupied(obstacle.box_at(0.0))
grid.compute_clearance()
path = fp.plan_hybrid_astar(grid, fp.FreeSpacePose(x, y, yaw), goal, vehicle, fp.FreeSpaceConfig())
traj = fp.free_space_trajectory(path, v0, fp.FreeSpaceConfig(), 0.1)

rec = SceneRecorder("run.mcap")              # or SceneRecorder(live=True) for ws://localhost:8765
rec.lanes((road_map.lane(i).left, road_map.lane(i).right) for i in road_map.lane_ids())
rec.frame(t, ego, vehicle, [obstacle_dict(o) for o in obstacles], out, "fiss_plus")

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
ctrl = fp.make_controller("mpc", vehicle)       # or "stanley_pid"
car = fp.KinematicBicycle(vehicle, ego)
car.step(ctrl.compute(car.state, out.trajectory, t_since_plan), 0.05)

docs.title: ROS 1 / ROS 2
docs.text:
Both wrappers are thin: the same LocalPlanner runs inside, planning is timer driven (or on every odometry message with plan_on_odom), and configuration changes are applied between cycles.

ROS 2 ROS 1 ros2 launch fiss_planner_ros2 planner.launch.py roslaunch fiss_planner_ros1 planner.launch ros2 param set /fiss_planner planner.type fiss rosrun dynamic_reconfigure dynparam set /fiss_planner planner_type fiss components PlannerNode, ControllerNode nodes planner_node, controller_node

The config_file parameter takes a YAML file in the core format (see Python): a preset from configs/ or a profile from python/fiss_planner/profiles/. ROS parameters override its values.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
Topic Type ~/odom nav_msgs/Odometry in ~/obstacles fiss_planner_msgs/ObstacleArray in ~/reference_path nav_msgs/Path in (path mode) ~/goal geometry_msgs/PoseStamped in (map mode) ~/stop_lines fiss_planner_msgs/StopLineStateArray in (traffic lights) ~/trajectory fiss_planner_msgs/Trajectory out: time-parameterized x, y, yaw, v, a, κ, s, d ~/path, ~/reference nav_msgs/Path out ~/stats fiss_planner_msgs/PlannerStats out: mode, timings, counts, blocking obstacle, gap / headway / TTC to the vehicle ahead ~/candidates visualization_msgs/MarkerArray out (publish_candidates) ~/markers visualization_msgs/MarkerArray out (ROS 2): ego, obstacles, predicted paths; vehicle ahead and blocking obstacle highlighted

Obstacles use fiss_planner_msgs/ObstacleArray: a rectangular footprint per object plus a predicted trajectory (times relative to the header stamp). A single state with is_static describes a parked object. A single state without is_static (a tracked object with its current speed) gets a prediction according to prediction.mode: lane_following (default; along its lane of the Lanelet2 map, constant velocity without a map), constant_velocity, or as_given.

docs.title: Keeping distance
docs.text:
The safety envelope and the proximity costs (see Concepts) are parameters like any other and can be tuned live:

ros2 param set /fiss_planner cost.desired_time_headway 2.0
ros2 param set /fiss_planner safety.min_ttc 2.0
ros2 param set /fiss_planner safety.crossing_time_gap 1.0   # crossing / oncoming traffic

collision.ignore_rear_in_lane is on in the shipped configuration: followers in the ego's lane are expected to keep their distance. degraded_horizon sets the collision horizon of the retry before an emergency stop.

docs.title: Visualization and recording
docs.text:
ros2 launch fiss_planner_ros2 planner.launch.py rviz:=true opens RViz 2 with the reference, plan, candidates and scene markers. To record a run for Foxglove:

ros2 bag record -s mcap -o run /odom /perception/obstacles /tf \
    /fiss_planner/trajectory /fiss_planner/path /fiss_planner/stats \
    /fiss_planner/candidates /fiss_planner/markers

docs.title: Maps
docs.text: Set map.lanelet2_path (plus map.origin_lat/lon) to load a Lanelet2 map. Lane-change legality, speed limits and traffic-light stop lines come from the map and its routing graph. A goal on ~/goal computes the route, and its position is where the route's lane changes must be done. Without a map, publish ~/reference_path and set path.lane_width / path.num_left_lanes / path.num_right_lanes.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text: Odometry and obstacles may come in any frame with a TF to map_frame. Positions inside the planner refer to the vehicle box center; odom_to_center_offset is the distance from the odometry frame (e.g. rear-axle base_link) to the center along the heading.
